summary: Guderian bypasses an undefeated Tula. A German division’s panic, a Soviet breakout and orders to destroy civilian shelter reveal the military and human costs of the southern thrust.
body:
A city that still blocked the road

Tula remained an obstacle because its defenders continued to function. German forces could move around the city, threaten its communications, and reach settlements farther east without extinguishing the Soviet army and industrial community inside it. On 18 November 1941, Heinz Guderian renewed the southern offensive toward Moscow under precisely those conditions. His Second Panzer Army was expected to turn movement beyond Tula into the southern arm of a much larger envelopment. It would have to do so while containing a defended city behind its leading formations and protecting an increasingly exposed eastern flank.[1]

The opening produced a striking local advance. The U.S. Army history reports that one of Guderian's corps covered almost twenty-five miles during the first day. Read alone, that distance suggests the return of the mobile warfare that had carried German forces across enormous stretches of the Soviet Union. Read beside the condition of the army and the tasks still ahead, it becomes more ambiguous. A fast spearhead could reach a new objective before the infantry needed to secure the route, while the surviving Soviet positions continued to threaten the forces passing them. Tactical momentum and operational vulnerability grew together.[1]

Tula’s survival shaped the offensive from its first day. Guderian needed the routes through Stalinogorsk and Venev to reach the Kashira approaches, yet Fiftieth Army still held the city beside his line of advance. This study follows the renewed attack of 18 November through its late-November bypass and Soviet response; the final December attempt to close Tula’s encirclement belongs to The Limits of the Advance. Within that interval, the central problem was already visible. Guderian could send mobile formations north faster than he could remove the Soviet forces beside and behind them. The army’s vulnerability grew from those unfinished battles.[1]

The defence behind the name

The Fiftieth Army had survived the destruction of the Bryansk position in October in a badly damaged condition. Its defence of Tula drew on regular formations and local resources, including the Tula Workers' Regiment, the 156th NKVD Rifle Regiment, and the 108th Tank Division. These components were not interchangeable. Infantry, tanks, artillery, security troops, and workers organised for combat contributed different capabilities. Holding the city required them to function as parts of a defence rather than as a collection of heroic names. A surviving headquarters and a working system for issuing orders were as important as the determination to stand.[2][1]

On 10 November, the Fiftieth Army had come under Zhukov's Western Front. This brought Tula into the same front command responsible for the principal Moscow approaches and made the southern defence part of a broader allocation of forces. Command responsibility mattered because the danger did not stop at a city boundary. An enemy move east of Tula could threaten roads connecting neighbouring armies, while a Soviet counterattack near the Oka could prevent German forces farther west from helping Guderian. The local battle and the wider front therefore influenced one another even when their soldiers could not see the same battlefield.[1]

Tula's industrial role made this relationship unusually tangible. Evacuation had removed much of its productive capacity, yet remaining facilities continued to manufacture weapons and repair equipment. A factory could be part of national evacuation policy and still leave behind workers and machinery performing urgent local tasks. The distinction helps explain how a threatened industrial city could support its own defence while losing much of the economic activity that had defined it before the war. Production continued under military necessity and severe disruption, rather than under anything resembling ordinary factory conditions.[2]

A workers' regiment begins with a decision

The Tula City Defence Committee’s resolution of 23 October gave the Workers’ Regiment an institutional beginning. The surviving catalogue identifies the decision and its archival reference, but does not supply a complete record of the men’s enlistment, training or conduct. It cannot establish that every worker volunteered. Its narrower evidence is useful: the city authorities were organising labour for combat before the renewed November offensive. Keeping workshops functioning and forming a regiment were connected demands on the same community, not spontaneous expressions of an undifferentiated civilian will.[3]

Evacuation and local defence placed competing demands on Tula's workforce. Sending machinery east preserved future production; keeping skilled workers and usable equipment in the city supported the soldiers defending it now. The workers' regiment added another demand for men who might otherwise have remained in a workshop. Tula's industrial contribution consequently included both the plant that left and the repairs or manufacture that continued. Its inhabitants were caught inside these decisions, maintaining an endangered city while parts of the community departed. The defence drew strength from that work, but it also consumed the labour and resources on which civilian life depended.[3][2]

The bypass opens

Guderian’s postwar study describes the assignments that dispersed his army on 18 November. Eighteenth Panzer Division went toward Yefremov, where he places street fighting two days later. Tenth Motorised Division moved toward Yepifan and Mikhaylov, while Twenty-Ninth Motorised Division covered the eastern flank against forces expected from the Ryazan–Kolomna area. These were supporting operations essential to the main thrust. Their directions explain why listing twelve divisions under Second Panzer Army does not establish that twelve divisions were available to attack the same objective. Guderian distributed them across a widening front and later used that exposure to explain the offensive’s failure.[4]

The names on that itinerary describe different problems. Stalinogorsk lay in the industrial country east of Tula; Venev offered a route farther north; Kashira stood on the Oka system and mattered for movement toward the capital's southern approaches. Reaching one place did not secure the others. Nor could a force directed toward an Oka crossing assume that the surrounding roads and rear areas were safe. A column's position on a map might look like the beginning of an encirclement while the space behind it still contained organised Soviet troops capable of fighting, withdrawing, or striking its communications.[1][4]

The Germans were still trying to remove the consequences of their October approach. Guderian recalled that on 29 October there had been enough fuel for only one tank battalion in the leading force; a battalion of the Grossdeutschland infantry regiment rode on the tanks. The attempt to take Tula by a sudden assault failed with heavy losses. He also described the Orel–Tula road deteriorating under traffic and wet weather. These are a defeated commander’s later explanations, but they identify specific inherited problems: an intact Soviet defence, worn transport and a damaged principal road. The November bypass began before those problems had been resolved.[4]

Fresh Soviet troops complicated the advance almost immediately. The 239th Rifle Division entered the fighting around Stalinogorsk and contested the area through which German formations were attempting to move north. Its presence forced the attackers to fight for their route and then attempt another encirclement before they could turn fully toward their larger objectives. Guderian's account acknowledges the division's resistance and its later escape. The episode is especially revealing because his explanation was intended to describe German operational problems: even there, Soviet troops appear as an active opponent disrupting the sequence of the advance, rather than a force simply waiting for the winter to intervene.[2][4]

On 17 November, according to Guderian, fresh Soviet troops near Uzlovaya and tanks advancing from Dedilovo broke the cohesion of the 112th Infantry Division. He described panic spreading toward Bogoroditsk and the neighbouring 167th Division helping to restore the situation. That admission matters, but his description cannot establish the motives of every retreating soldier. It records a battlefield breakdown under pressure, not a documented collective refusal of orders or mutiny. His further claim that this was the campaign’s first such panic is not demonstrable from the account. Soviet action exposed the division’s weakness; a neighbouring formation’s intervention helped prevent a wider collapse.[4]

The episode was followed by a requirement for relief. The 112th Division could no longer be treated as a dependable addition to the main attack merely because it retained a divisional headquarters. Guderian records plans to bring the 56th Infantry Division forward from Karachev. The relief still had to travel, take over ground and release troops from existing tasks. This was how loss of cohesion affected an operation beyond the men immediately involved. It altered the disposition of formations elsewhere and reduced the reserves available for the next unexpected Soviet attack. The record gives no basis for adding a punishment or execution total to the incident.[4]

The 239th Rifle Division’s escape later in November exposed another weakness in the German method. Guderian acknowledged that the enclosing line, particularly the sector held by Twenty-Ninth Motorised Division, was thin. In his account, the Soviet troops broke through during the night following the entries for 27 November, leaving artillery and equipment but saving men and inflicting serious German losses. The episode was a costly escape, not an untouched division marching out intact. It nevertheless denied the attackers the destruction they sought. Soviet soldiers who escaped capture also escaped immediate exposure to Germany’s lethal prisoner system; their survival had consequences beyond the next strength return.[4][9]

The bypass was accompanied by disagreement over its destination. Guderian says he went to Bock on the evening of 24 November to request an attainable mission, describing exhausted infantry, poor supply and the exposed eastern flank. Bock communicated similar concerns upward, but Brauchitsch insisted that the offensive continue and identified the Mikhaylov–Zaraysk line and disruption of the Ryazan–Kolomna railway as objectives. This is Guderian’s retrospective presentation of his own objections. It should be read alongside his continuing orders to attack Tula. Protest at headquarters did not end the operation or relieve its commander of responsibility for how his formations were employed.[4]

The projected strike against Soviet communications provides another measure of the operation’s limits. Guderian’s retrospective account records the importance attached to cutting the Ryazan–Kolomna railway, which supported the Soviet position beyond his eastern flank. After reaching Mikhaylov on 27 November, the Tenth Motorised Division sent reconnaissance and demolition parties toward that railway, but they did not reach the intended target. This later development clarifies the ambition behind the movement that began on 18 November. Taking an intermediate town and dispatching a patrol were steps toward disrupting Soviet reinforcement; they were not proof that the railway had been severed. The distinction preserves the difference between an operational order, a reconnaissance effort, and an achieved interdiction.[4]

A flank is an obligation

The central difficulty was the shape of Guderian's advance. His leading troops were being directed northward, but Soviet forces could approach their eastern side from the Ryazan and Kolomna directions. Second Army, farther south, could not simply provide an unbroken protective wall, while Fourth Army had its own difficulties around the Oka. The farther the Second Panzer Army advanced, the longer the vulnerable side of its operation became. Protecting it required troops, reconnaissance, and reserves that were also needed for the main attack. Guderian's later emphasis on this problem was self-interested, but the geography and the continuing Soviet activity made it real.[4][1]

West of Tula, Guderian's Forty-Third Army Corps faced a different task from the mobile troops racing east. Its Thirty-First and 131st Infantry Divisions operated between the Upa and Oka, with Aleksin among the relevant approaches. Their advance was supposed to help reduce Tula and connect the operation toward Fourth Army. Meanwhile, formations on the opposite side of the city had to cover approaches from Ryazan and Kolomna. The army was trying to compress one flank around a defended city while extending the other into open country. The infantry needed for the first task could not simply be transferred to the second without weakening the attempted encirclement.[4]

Kluge’s Fourth Army offered little prospect of repairing the northern connection. Soviet counterblows near Serpukhov kept it engaged, and its commander reported severely depleted regiments. Guderian’s design nevertheless required cooperation across the Oka and toward Aleksin. The armies’ difficulties were therefore cumulative: one command could receive an instruction to connect with a neighbour whose own battle prevented it from reaching the meeting ground. This was a problem of available force and timing. Describing it simply as insufficient aggression by Kluge reproduces the rivalry between commanders without explaining why the projected connection failed.[1]

German success had often depended on accepting flank risks in order to dislocate an opponent before he could respond. In November, however, Soviet resistance was surviving long enough for the consequences of that risk to accumulate. The Fiftieth Army remained at Tula, the Oka remained a significant barrier, and fresh Soviet forces were being directed toward the endangered approaches. Continued advance could therefore enlarge an army's commitments without correspondingly reducing the enemy's capacity to interfere. The operational method depended increasingly on an enemy collapse that had yet to occur.[1]

Shelter as a military resource

The harshness of the southern battle reached into civilian homes. On 17 November, the Stavka issued Order No. 0428 directing the destruction of settlements behind German lines to deprive the invaders of shelter. It authorised aircraft, artillery, and small raiding parties, and instructed Soviet forces withdrawing from an area to take the population with them while destroying places the enemy could use. The order's premise was that accommodation had become a resource on which German endurance depended. Its human implications were equally clear: houses and villages could be sacrificed in the pursuit of military advantage.[6]

Order No. 0428 prescribed destruction forty to sixty kilometres behind the German front and twenty to thirty kilometres to either side of roads. Regiments were to form raiding parties of twenty to thirty men, selected for physical courage and political reliability, and successful participants could be recommended for decorations. The order mobilised military discipline and reward around the destruction of inhabited places. Its distances specify the intended area of action; they are not a record of villages actually burned. The evacuation clause applied to Soviet withdrawals and supplies no proof that every threatened household could leave with food, transport or shelter arranged.[6]

The order also required reports every three days naming the places destroyed and the means used. A later Western Front report, dated 29 November and signed by Zhukov and Bulganin, claimed 398 settlements burned or destroyed. Its published translation attributes most of this activity to raiding and diversionary groups, citing poor weather and a shortage of incendiary shells as limits on air and artillery action. This is evidence of reported implementation, not an independently audited village total. The inspected reproductions do not establish how many inhabitants were evacuated or killed. They therefore support a more serious conclusion than an order left on paper, without permitting invented measures of its civilian cost.[10]

German occupation made shelter a contested resource before Soviet raiding parties arrived. The destruction order described German troops expelling villagers from buildings they wanted for their own use; that is the issuing command’s account, not a locality-by-locality investigation. Its response was to make those buildings unavailable. Civilians could consequently face dispossession under occupation and the destruction of their homes by forces seeking to deny accommodation to the occupier. The two acts require their own evidence and responsibility. Their conjunction explains why a discussion of winter limited to tanks, uniforms and temperatures leaves out people whose houses had become military objectives.[6]

Toward Kashira and the counterstroke

The advance beyond 18 November developed through several further engagements. German forces pushed through the country east of Tula and toward the approaches to Kashira, while Soviet commanders attempted to contain the penetration. It is important to keep these subsequent events in sequence. The threat to Kashira belongs to the later November fighting; it was not a completed achievement of the opening day. The Seventeenth Panzer Division's northward movement helped form the large bulge around Tula described in the official history, but the city continued to resist inside the threatened arc.[1]

Pavel Belov's cavalry corps helped oppose the later threat to Kashira, alongside tank and infantry forces. On 26 November his Second Cavalry Corps became the First Guards Cavalry Corps, a redesignation publicly announced in Pravda the following day. The award recognised an existing formation, not the sudden assembly of a new corps. Cavalry gave Soviet commanders a means of moving armed men where motor transport was scarce, but successful action still depended on support, ammunition and coordination. Belov's troops contested the approaches on which Guderian's northern movement depended. Their intervention threatened a spearhead already connected to its rear by an increasingly vulnerable stretch of road.[7][1]

An army still arriving

The Tenth Army would eventually strengthen the region beyond Guderian's eastern flank, but its movement belonged to the last week of November. Its commander, Filipp Golikov, received marching orders on 24 November. The army had to cover the long journey from Syzran by rail and on foot because it possessed little motor transport. Its appearance on a strategic map therefore represented a process unfolding over days. A headquarters assignment could precede the arrival of all the troops needed to carry it out.[1]

This sequence explains why German commanders could experience Soviet strength as a succession of unwelcome surprises. The reinforcements did not have to arrive everywhere at once to frustrate an offensive. A new force at a threatened crossing could prevent an immediate success; another formation farther east could make an exposed flank harder to ignore. German troops then spent additional time and ammunition solving problems outside their original objective. Soviet reinforcement was uneven and costly, but its cumulative effect was to deprive the attacker of the uninterrupted sequence on which his larger design depended.[1]

What the southern advance meant

By late November, Guderian’s army had fought its way into a broad salient east of Tula without eliminating the city’s defenders. The difference from the opening day was cumulative. The 112th Division needed relief; the 239th Rifle Division had escaped an enclosure; the railway interdiction had failed; and the Kashira thrust encountered a Soviet response. Each event changed what the army could attempt next. The offensive remained dangerous, but it no longer offered a continuous sequence of opportunities. The Germans were spending their remaining strength revisiting tasks that the original plan had assumed would already be completed.[4][1]

The wider war was also moving on 18 November. Britain opened Operation Crusader in North Africa, adding pressure in another theatre while Anglo-American assistance to the Soviet Union developed. That operation was not an immediate rescue for a particular Soviet battalion near Tula, and it should not be inserted into the local battle as though it were. It did, however, underline the German strategic problem: the eastern campaign was continuing while other commitments remained active. German planning could no longer assume that defeating the Soviet Union would quickly release its resources for a different war.[8][5]

Tula’s defenders had preserved a city that could still sustain an army, repair equipment and obstruct the German approach. That achievement included withdrawals and local defeats; the survival of the defence depended on keeping enough organisation intact through them. It also depended on civilians whose work was redirected toward military needs and whose homes could be sacrificed to them. The late-November result was consequently both a military success for the Soviet defence and an unfinished emergency for its people. Guderian had gained positions from which he could try again. He had not obtained the secure southern arm of an encirclement of Moscow.[2][1]

Later attempts to close the ring would continue into December and belong to the study of the advance's limits. Meanwhile, farther south, German forces were approaching a different city whose capture appeared to promise a major strategic gain. The fall of Rostov would test another version of the same question: whether the army taking an important place could also secure the conditions necessary to hold it.[1]

sourceMethod: Numbered notes connect the prose to specific inspected passages. The U.S. Army campaign history is a retrospective synthesis, assessed alongside Soviet documentary transcriptions, institutional accounts and scholarship. Guderian’s and German signals officers’ postwar explanations are attributed; their criticisms of higher command are not independent proof of their own conduct. Public Cambridge extracts, edited diary selections and catalogue-only evidence are identified in the locators. Russian and German material is paraphrased in English; uninspected archival originals are not claimed as consulted. Orders, reported implementation and independently established outcomes remain distinct. Operational analysis is Ostkrieg’s interpretation of the cited evidence. This local editorial revision does not validate or update the companion maps or their cached passages.
